channel.title: Music_generation on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Music_generation on Best of AI

item.title: Soundful
item.description:
Soundful helps creators find music without licensing hassles. A user picks a genre, mood, and tempo, and the platform generates a track that can be customized and downloaded. The pitch is that each track is unique and cleared for use in videos, streams, and podcasts.

It serves YouTubers, streamers, marketers, and podcasters who need background music at scale. Different plans set what usage rights apply, including for monetized content and for commercial work.

item.title: AIVA
item.description: AIVA, short for Artificial Intelligence Virtual Artist, was built to compose music, with an early emphasis on classical and cinematic styles. You pick a style from a library of hundreds, set the length and key, and it generates a track. You can also upload an audio or MIDI file as an influence, or define your own chord progression. Video creators, game developers, podcasters, and advertisers use it to get background music without hiring a composer.

item.title: Beatoven.ai
item.description: Beatoven.ai is aimed at video makers, podcasters, and game developers who need background music without searching a stock library. You describe the track you want, such as a calm acoustic piece for a travel vlog, or choose a genre, mood, and duration, and the AI composes an original piece. You can change the emotion of different sections along the timeline, which is helpful when a video moves from a tense moment to a resolved one.

item.title: Boomy
item.description: Boomy is one of the easiest ways to generate music. You pick a style such as lo-fi, electronic, rap beats, or cinematic, and the system composes a track in moments. You can then adjust it by changing the arrangement, adding vocals or effects, and recording your own voice over the music. It requires no musical knowledge, which is why it appeals to casual creators and people who want custom background tracks.

item.title: Loudly
item.description:
Loudly offers music for people who need soundtracks without composing. Users can create tracks by choosing a genre, mood, and tempo, or by describing what they want in a prompt, and then download the result. A library of ready-made AI tracks lets you browse by genre and use case. It is intended for video creators, podcasters, streamers, game developers, and businesses that need background music.

Several features support practical use. A personalization option adjusts elements like instruments and structure, stems can be downloaded for editing, and an API allows developers to embed music generation in their own products, such as apps that need adaptive soundtracks. The company positions its music as safe for commercial use, with licenses that cover content on social platforms.

item.title: Jammable
item.description:
Jammable, formerly Voicify, lets people hear songs sung in a different voice. A user chooses a voice model from a library, uploads a vocal or song, and the system converts it so it sounds like the chosen voice. Fans and creators use it for parodies, mashups, and experiments.

The technology raises serious legal and ethical issues. Voices of real artists are protected in many places, and music labels and artists have objected to unauthorized voice clones. Sharing such covers can violate copyright and rights of publicity, and platforms may remove them. Use voices you have permission to use, and avoid presenting synthetic songs as the real artist.

item.title: Musicfy
item.description:
Musicfy offers several music tools in one place. Users can generate a track from a text prompt, convert one instrument or vocal to another voice or sound, separate a song into stems, and create voice covers with AI voices. It is aimed at creators who want to experiment with songs without a studio.

The same tools raise rights questions. Copying a real artist’s voice without permission can violate publicity and copyright rules, and platforms and labels remove such content. Generated music has varying licensing terms, so read them before releasing or monetizing songs.

item.title: Riffusion
item.description:
Riffusion started as a research demo that generated music clips by running Stable Diffusion on spectrogram images, an early sign that diffusion models could make audio. It grew into a platform where users type a prompt and get a song with vocals, and into a chat-like agent that helps produce tracks.

The brand changed to Producer.ai, and reports say it has since moved under Google’s music efforts, so product names and features may keep changing. Users should check the current site and how their saved songs and rights are handled through any transition.

item.title: Splice
item.description:
Splice supplies the building blocks of modern production. Producers search a huge catalog of samples by genre, key, and tempo, preview them in sync with their project, and download them under a license that allows use in released music. Plugin subscriptions let users rent instruments and effects.

AI features assist with creativity. Tools suggest compatible samples, and apps generate loops and ideas. Cloud project backup and collaboration features help producers work with others.

item.title: Stable Audio
item.description:
Stable Audio generates sound from descriptions. A user types a prompt such as an upbeat electronic track with a driving bass line, and the model produces a piece of the requested length. It can also create sound effects and ambient textures.

The models were trained on licensed audio, which Stability emphasizes to address rights concerns. Producers and sound designers use it for sketching ideas, backing tracks, and game audio. Smaller open models can run locally.

item.title: Mubert
item.description:
Mubert generates music in real time. You pick a mood, genre, or activity, such as focus, workout, or sleep, and it streams a continuous track that does not loop in an obvious way. Creators use it for background music in videos, streams, podcasts, and apps, and the royalty-free licensing makes it practical for online content.

Several products serve different needs. Mubert Render lets users create tracks of a chosen length from a text prompt or style, and a mobile app offers streaming for listening. An API allows developers to add generated music to games, fitness apps, and other products, delivering music that adapts to context. Artists can contribute sounds to the system, with revenue sharing for contributors.

item.title: Soundraw
item.description:
Soundraw makes custom background music for creators. You select parameters such as mood, genre, theme, tempo, and length, and the AI generates a number of options. You can then adjust the track in an editor, changing the intensity of different sections and instruments to match the pacing of a video, and download the result. This is more flexible than browsing a fixed stock library.

It’s aimed at content creators, marketers, filmmakers, and developers who need affordable music. The subscription offers unlimited downloads and a license for use on social platforms and in commercial projects, with protections against copyright claims on the creator’s own content. The tracks are made from music produced by in-house artists, and Soundraw positions the training data as licensed.

item.title: Suno
item.description: Suno made AI music accessible. You describe the song you want, such as an upbeat pop track about a road trip, or paste your own lyrics, and Suno produces complete songs with singing and instrumentation in under a minute. Users can choose styles and genres, extend and edit songs, create covers, and make instrumentals. It has been used for demos, background music, parody, and just for fun by people with no musical training.

item.title: Udio
item.description:
Udio produces music with an emphasis on audio quality and handling of lyrics. You describe a song or supply lyrics, and Udio generates clips that you can extend into full tracks, remix, and edit section by section. Users liked it for realistic vocals and for the control it gives over structure, and it has been used for songwriting ideas, demos, and entertainment.

Its path changed after legal disputes with major record labels. Udio reached licensing agreements with some labels and moved toward a platform where creation and sharing happen inside the service, often described as a walled garden, with limits on downloading tracks. Plans to build tools around licensed music mean terms can continue to change, and the experience differs from earlier versions, which let users download freely.
